In mathematics, a norm is a function in [[vector space|vector spaces]] with certain special properties.

== Conventional definition in inner product spaces ==

By convention, in [[inner product space]] $V$, the norm of a vector $v \in V$, denoted $\left\| v \right\|$, is defined:

$$
\| v \| = \sqrt{\langle v, v \rangle}
$$

== Formal definition in all vector spaces ==

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{F}$.

Map

$$
\begin{aligned} 
\| \cdot \|: V &\to \mathbb{R}\\ 
v &\mapsto \| v \| 
\end{aligned}
$$

is a '''norm''' on $V$ if 3 conditions are satisfied:

* '''Definiteness''': $\forall v\in V,\; \left\| v \right\|=0 \iff v=\vec 0$;
* '''Homogeneity''': $\forall a\in\mathbb{F},\;\forall v\in V,\; \left\| av \right\|=|a|\left\| v \right\|$;
* '''Triangle inequality''': $\forall v,w\in V,\; \left\| v+w \right\|\le \left\| v \right\|+\left\| w \right\|$
<ref>{{#cite:Q1920}}</ref>

<blockquote>
Notice the conventional definition $\| v \| = \sqrt{\langle v, v \rangle}$ is a special case of the mathematical definition.
</blockquote>

== Derived properties ==

=== Positive definiteness ===

$$\forall v \in V, \| v \|\ge 0$$

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\| v \| = \frac{1}{2}(2\| v \|)= \frac{1}{2}(\| v \| + \| -v \|) \\
\stackrel{\text{Triangle inequality}}{\ge} \frac{1}{2}\| v-v \| = 0
$$
{{End hidden}}
